principles: Naming a fault plainly and once
Damage done to other people's belief
Why the news comes before the event

world_behind.title: Corianton was on the Zoramite mission
world_behind.text: Alma 31:7 lists him with Shiblon among those Alma took to Antionum. What happened there is given only in this chapter.

world_behind.title: He left the ministry mid-mission
world_behind.text: Verse 3 says he forsook it and went to Siron after Isabel. Alma calls the abandonment grievous before he says anything about the woman.

world_behind.title: Isabel is named
world_behind.text: Verse 3 gives her name and calls her a harlot, and verse 4 says she stole away the hearts of many. She is one of a handful of women the record names at all.

world_behind.title: The comparison to Shiblon opens the charge
world_behind.text: Verse 1 asks whether Corianton has observed his brother's steadiness. Alma 38 had just praised that steadiness to Shiblon himself.

world_behind.title: The ranking of sins is stated carefully
world_behind.text: Verse 5 puts this abomination below shedding innocent blood and below denying the Holy Ghost. Verse 6 then defines the unpardonable sin as denial against knowledge.

world_behind.title: The public cost is named
world_behind.text: Verse 11 says the Zoramites would not believe Alma's words once they saw Corianton's conduct. The chapter treats a private sin as a public event.

world_behind.title: Corianton had a question
world_behind.text: Verse 17 says he marvels why these things should be known so long beforehand. The last three verses begin an answer that runs through Alma 42.

words.text: A land on the Lamanite borders. The name occurs once in scripture and is never described. Alma names it as the place his son went, which fixes the abandonment of the ministry to a specific journey.
A woman named once in scripture. The record gives her name, her trade, and the fact that many hearts followed her. Alma names her to his son directly and then says she is no excuse.

Beyond forgiveness. The word occurs twice in this record and never in the King James Bible; the other use is Sherem in Jacob 7, fearing he has committed it. Alma defines it as a denial of the Holy Ghost once it has taken hold in you, made in full knowledge.
Treated at 2 Nephi 9:47, where Jacob asks whether he should harrow up his hearers' souls. Alma uses the same figure of tearing ground open, and says he would not do it to his son except for his good.

To go against, to thwart. The phrase "cross yourself" (v. 9) occurs twice in this record, both in this verse, and never in the King James Bible. Alma repeats it in the same breath, which makes it an instruction to act against your own wants.

Good news announced. The record uses the phrase eleven times and the King James Bible four, including Paul on the feet of those who bring it (Rom. 10:15). Alma uses it three times in five verses, and it is the ministry Corianton walked away from.

phrases.term: Have ye not observed the steadiness of thy brother
phrases.text: Alma opens by pointing at Shiblon. He had praised the same quality to Shiblon's face one chapter earlier (Alma 38:2), and he now uses it as the measure for the son who is being corrected.

phrases.term: Thou didst go on unto boasting in thy strength and thy wisdom
phrases.text: The first fault named, and it is pride rather than the sin everyone remembers. Alma 38 had warned Shiblon against exactly this, and here it is described as something that already happened.
The charge stated before Isabel is mentioned. Alma puts the desertion first in the sentence, which orders the offense by the trust broken rather than by the act.

phrases.term: But this was no excuse for thee, my son
phrases.text: Alma grants that Isabel drew many and refuses it as mitigation in the same verse. The concession and the refusal sit side by side.

phrases.term: Most abominable above all sins save it be the shedding of innocent blood or denying the Holy Ghost
phrases.text: A ranking with two things above it. Alma is precise about the position rather than absolute about the severity, and verse 6 explains the two exceptions.

phrases.term: I would not dwell upon your crimes, to harrow up your soul, if it were not for your good
phrases.text: Alma states his reason for saying any of this. He names the pain he is causing and the purpose of causing it, and he does not repeat the charge after verse 11.

phrases.term: Cross yourself in all these things
phrases.text: The instruction, given twice in one verse. Alma asks for action against his son's own inclination, and pairs it with an end to chasing what the eye wants.

phrases.term: Counsel with your elder brothers in your undertakings
phrases.text: A command, not a suggestion. Alma tells his youngest that he is in his youth and stands in need of being nourished by his brothers, and gives him Helaman and Shiblon as the ones to ask.

phrases.term: When they saw your conduct they would not believe in my words
phrases.text: The cost of the sin, stated as its effect on other people's belief. Alma had been preaching in Antionum; his son's conduct is named as a reason the preaching failed there.

phrases.term: Return unto them, and acknowledge your faults and that wrong which ye have done
phrases.text: Repentance is given a public step. Alma tells him to go back to the people he damaged and say what he did, which is more than an inward turn to the Lord.

phrases.term: Is not a soul at this time as precious unto God as a soul will be at the time of his coming?
phrases.text: Alma answers his son's question with a question. Three verses ask whether present souls, present knowledge, and present angels are worth less than future ones, and the assumed answer carries the argument.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: A rebuke that begins by naming the standard
verses.text: The chapter opens by measuring one son against another and does it twice. Verse 1 asks "have ye not observed the steadiness of thy brother, his faithfulness, and his diligence in keeping the commandments of God?" Verse 2 draws the comparison directly: "thou didst not give so much heed unto my words as did thy brother, among the people of the Zoramites." The previous chapter is the standard being applied, and the two chapters were spoken to two sons about the same mission. The rebuke's first move is to point at a document the reader has just finished.

verses.label: v. 3–4
verses.title: The excuse stated before it is refused
verses.text: The charge is specific, and it comes with the mitigation attached: Corianton "did go over into the land of Siron among the borders of the Lamanites, after the harlot Isabel," and then "she did steal away the hearts of many; but this was no excuse for thee, my son." The concession is real and the record makes it in the father's own voice before dismissing it. Isabel is named once in the volume, in verse 3, and nothing else about her is reported anywhere.

verses.label: v. 5–6
verses.title: Offences ranked in the middle of a reprimand
verses.text: The rebuke stops to rank offences. The sin is "most abominable above all sins save it be the shedding of innocent blood or denying the Holy Ghost," which names two exceptions and puts the son's conduct third. Verse 6 then defines the second exception carefully, "if ye deny the Holy Ghost when it once has had place in you, and ye know that ye deny it," adding a condition of knowledge, and appends a fourth case about murder against the light. A father angry with a son gives four categories and their boundaries.

verses.label: v. 7–8
verses.title: The speaker explains his own method
verses.text: Two verses interrupt the reproach to say why it is being made: "I would not dwell upon your crimes, to harrow up your soul, if it were not for your good." Then the reason it cannot be dropped: "ye cannot hide your crimes from God; and except ye repent they will stand as a testimony against you at the last day." The record preserves not just a rebuke but a justification for the rebuke's severity, addressed to the person receiving it.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: A command quoted as dictation
verses.text: The instruction is not given in the father's own authority. It is reported: "the Spirit of the Lord doth say unto me: Command thy children to do good, lest they lead away the hearts of many people to destruction; therefore I command you, my son." Two commands stand together here, one received and one issued, and the second is presented as obedience to the first. The verse supplies the chain rather than the conclusion.

verses.label: v. 17–19
verses.title: Three questions, and no answer to any of them
verses.text: The chapter's last three verses are all interrogative and all built on the same frame: "is not a soul at this time as precious unto God as a soul will be at the time of his coming?", "Is it not as necessary that the plan of redemption should be made known unto this people as well as unto their children?", "Is it not as easy at this time for the Lord to send his angel to declare these glad tidings unto us as unto our children?" Six question marks stand in this chapter and half of them are here. None is answered, and the chapter ends on the third.

chapter.title: The chapter opens on pride and closes on doctrine
chapter.text: The sexual sin occupies three verses in the middle. Alma names boasting first and spends the last five verses on the coming of Christ.

chapter.title: The desertion is the charge
chapter.text: Verse 3 says forsake the ministry before it says anything about Isabel. Alma orders the offense by what was entrusted rather than by what was done.

chapter.title: He grants the mitigating fact and refuses it
chapter.text: She stole away the hearts of many, and that was no excuse. Alma does not dispute the circumstance; he denies that it changes the responsibility.

chapter.title: The ranking has two things above it
chapter.text: Alma is careful enough to define both exceptions, and careful enough to say that murder against knowledge is hard to be forgiven without calling it impossible.

chapter.title: He names the pain and the reason for it
chapter.text: Verse 7 says he would not harrow up his son's soul except for his good, and he keeps to that: the accusation stops at verse 11 and never returns.

chapter.title: The worst consequence is other people's unbelief
chapter.text: Verse 11 makes the Zoramites who would not hear Alma the measure of the damage. A private failure is weighed by its public effect.

chapter.title: Repentance includes going back
chapter.text: Turning to the Lord is verse 13's first half; returning to the people and acknowledging the wrong is its second. Alma requires both.

chapter.title: The correction ends by answering a question
chapter.text: Corianton marvels at the timing of prophecy, and Alma takes it seriously enough to begin an answer that occupies three more chapters.

applications.title: Do not open with the comparison
applications.text: Alma begins by pointing at the brother, "have ye not observed the steadiness of thy brother," and it is the least effective sentence in the chapter. The record keeps it, and it is worth noticing how quickly a correction that starts with a sibling stops being about the fault.

applications.title: Refuse the excuse without disputing the fact
applications.text: Isabel really did steal away the hearts of many, and Alma grants it in the same breath as he rejects it, "but this was no excuse for thee, my son. Thou shouldst have tended to the ministry wherewith thou wast entrusted." Conceding the circumstance costs nothing and removes the argument.

applications.title: Name the fault once and stop
applications.text: Alma says what he has to say and then says why he is stopping, "I would not dwell upon your crimes, to harrow up your soul, if it were not for your good." Correction has a purpose and the purpose sets its length.

applications.title: Give the instruction as a set of verbs
applications.text: Repent, forsake, go no more, cross yourself in all these things. Four actions, all of them things the son can begin that day. What ends the diagnosis in this chapter is a to-do list.

applications.title: Ask your siblings
applications.text: Alma commands his youngest to "counsel with your elder brothers in your undertakings," giving the reason plainly, "thou art in thy youth, and ye stand in need to be nourished by your brothers." Naming who a person should consult is part of a useful correction.

applications.title: Count the damage to other people
applications.text: The heaviest sentence in the chapter concerns the effect more than the act, "when they saw your conduct they would not believe in my words." Ask what your conduct has cost somebody else's willingness to listen.

applications.title: Go back to the people you damaged
applications.text: Turning to God is not the whole instruction, "but rather return unto them, and acknowledge your faults and that wrong which ye have done." The repair runs through the people who were affected.

applications.title: Answer the intellectual question too
applications.text: Corianton also had a genuine puzzle about why Christ's coming was known so far in advance, and Alma answers it, "is not a soul at this time as precious unto God as a soul will be at the time of his coming?" A moral correction that ignores the person's real question leaves half the work undone.

questions.text: Whose steadiness have I noticed and never learned from?
Where have I boasted in my own strength lately?
What have I been entrusted with that I have quietly stopped tending?
What true circumstance am I using as an excuse?
What would crossing myself look like this week?
Who has stopped believing something because of how I acted?
Who do I owe an acknowledgment to?
